extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math historians, Math.SE readers, and mathematically literate general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and correct a historical/mathematical misconception (here: what Cauchy actually claimed about continuity), distinguishing precise mathematical statements and contextual definitions. Targeted exposition that evaluates historical claims with examples and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sequence versus series
rubrics_metrics.description: The confusion arises from a perennially confusing piece of mathematical terminology: a convergent sequence is not at all the same as a convergent series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that Cauchy's claim concerns a convergent series S(x)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty f_i(x), not a convergent sequence f_\infty(x)=\lim_{i\to\infty} f_i(x). The premise 'the sum converges' is stronger than pointwise convergence of a sequence, so statements about series do not automatically transfer to sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurately report the original claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy never claimed that a convergent sequence of continuous functions has a continuous limit; his claim was about convergent series of continuous functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing historical texts, quote or closely paraphrase the original wording; avoid replacing the original claim with a different (and easier-to-disprove) assertion. The post notes many modern sources misstate Cauchy's claim as the false 'pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous functions is always continuous.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete counterexamples for universal continuity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone asserts that pointwise limits of continuous functions are always continuous, present simple counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: f_n(x)=x^n on [-1,1] (limit discontinuous on [0,1]); bump functions narrowing to a spike (e^{-x^2/n} converges to 1 at 0 and 0 elsewhere). Use explicit sequences to show failure of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check historical definitions and context before judging errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g., of continuity) and accepted meanings can change over time, so an assertion that someone 'made a mistake' should account for period terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider scholarship (e.g., Lakatos) that argues Cauchy's theorem may be correct under the 1821 concept of continuity. Investigate how contemporaries understood the terms and whether objections arose at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate plausibility by considering elementary counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: It is implausible that Cauchy would have overlooked extremely simple counterexamples to a claimed theorem; historical claims of such errors should be scrutinized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a purported mistake would have been trivial to detect (e.g., x^n), question secondary sources that attribute such an error to a prominent mathematician without evidence. Use the existence and simplicity of counterexamples as a plausibility check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine reception and timing of critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at when objections or counterexamples to an asserted theorem first appeared in the literature as evidence about whether an original author truly erred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes nobody complained about Cauchy's controversial theorem until 1847; delayed criticism may indicate a difference in definitions rather than a straightforward mistake. Check historical timeline of responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid careless restatement and secondary-source propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary sources often propagate a mistaken restatement of an original claim (replacing it with a different, wrong assertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely only on modern summaries (e.g., Wikipedia, nLab) without checking primary sources. The author criticizes repeated misstatements that convert Cauchy's series claim into the false sequence-claim; use primary texts to prevent this anti-pattern.
